messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael is a 49-year-old city council member who has been married for over twenty years. He had served two tours of duty in Iraq, and the memory he carries most vividly is also the memory he cannot hold together. It comes from his second deployment, when a roadside detonation tore through the lead vehicle of his convoy. He remembers the heat, the ringing, the shouting—but the seconds just before and just after are a smear of black static. He can see a hand, someone’s hand, reaching for him through the smoke, and he knows that hand belonged to a man who did not make it, but he cannot say for sure if he reached back. When he tries to tell his wife about it, he loses the thread mid-sentence, his mouth going dry, and he shakes his head and walks away. The terror that seizes him in those moments is the same terror he felt in the dust and noise—it has never dimmed or faded.

At home, Michael keeps the television on almost constantly, volume high enough to fill the rooms. He does this because quiet leaves space for his own thoughts, and his own thoughts frighten him. He has come to believe that if he does not monitor what passes through his mind, he might drift into something uncontrollable—a panic, a breakdown, perhaps even a violent outburst. He checks himself all day, scanning for any thought that feels unhinged, any flicker of anger or disorientation that could be a sign he is going crazy. At night, sleep rarely comes easily, and when it does it is broken; often he lies awake staring at the ceiling, trying to keep his mind blank.

The world outside his front door feels like a threat he cannot lower his guard against. Even when his wife tells him the neighborhood is safe, that the city is quiet, he finds it impossible to believe her. Danger feels latent, everywhere, and he has to be vigilant at all times. His body seems to know this before his mind does: if his wife touches him from behind at the kitchen counter, he flinches violently, his heart slamming. He has started avoiding all physical contact with others. At city council meetings, he positions himself so that no one can approach him from the back. He no longer shakes hands with constituents, offering instead a tight nod and a step back. Some people have noticed, have asked if he is feeling unwell, and he makes vague excuses about a back injury.

The consequences have crept up slowly. He used to enjoy the public forums and town halls, the work of listening to people’s concerns. Now he dreads them. The crowded rooms, the sudden brushes of shoulders, the unexpected hand on his arm from a well-meaning supporter—each sends a jolt through him that takes minutes to settle. He has delegated two committee meetings to a deputy this month, and last week he left a school board joint session early because the auditorium was too packed. His wife has grown quiet around him, careful not to startle him, and he can feel the distance widening between them though he does not know how to close it.

What finally brought Michael to seek help was a moment at a veteran’s day ceremony. He was standing at the back of the hall, trying to keep his composure, when an elderly man in a service cap clapped him on the shoulder without warning. Michael spun around, his arm raised in a defensive motion, and for a terrible second he saw the man’s face register shock and fear. He apologized profusely, but the shame stayed with him all day. That night, he told his wife he needed to talk to someone. He is terrified of what he might discover—that he is damaged beyond repair, that his mind is truly slipping—but he is also tired of living in a world that feels like a war zone, and he hopes, more than anything, that someone can show him how to feel safe again.
